post1-title.why: Plural, since there are several books. The 'Popular Science' label is now an icon.

post1-p1.text: More often than not, physics is taught as a collection of equations to memorize and plug numbers into. That picture could not be further from the truth. Science is done by humans (at least until recently; with the advent of AI the conversation gets much more complicated, and since many people are already chiming in, I will stay out of it here. See David Hogg's take (arXiv:2602.10181) for a great discussion). The train of thought behind a result, which can take decades and many failed attempts, is as important to learn as the material itself if you intend to pursue physics as a career.
post1-p1.why: 'to be memorized and to plug numbers into to obtain results' was clunky; 'till' → 'until'; the long parenthetical is split so it reads cleanly; 'that at times take' had a subject–verb mismatch.
post1-p1.idea: Ideas for an extra line: a specific moment when learning the history changed how you understood a topic, or the first book that hooked you.

post3-title.text: Incomplete and Incorrect Theories Should Be Encouraged

post3-p1.text: One thing that truly bothers me is how physics classes often move at a pace that strips away the years (or even decades) it took to develop not only a theory but also the intuition behind it. One of the most interesting examples, and one rarely discussed in undergraduate classes, is the history of the strong force. I stumbled upon it while reading the Wikipedia page on the Yukawa potential and its origins. Physicists wrestled with why the nucleus doesn't blow itself apart under the repulsion between its protons, and with whether the neutron is a composite particle (made up of an electron and a proton). Heisenberg, best known for his uncertainty principle, played a key role in refining our understanding of the strong force and in part inspired the work of Yukawa and later Fermi. Though his theory was incomplete and incorrect, it contained remarkable insights, such as isospin, and eventually paved the way to a coherent theory of the strong force. I truly see it as a necessary step in that development, and I think students should be encouraged to see incomplete and incorrect theories the same way: they are often a necessary step toward a coherent theory.
post3-p1.why: The first sentence had two verbs ('are structured … teach'); 'wiki' → 'Wikipedia'; 'People wrestled with the idea of why' tightened; the last two sentences repeated 'necessary step' and are now merged.
post3-p1.check: Fact check: Fermi's beta decay theory (late 1933, published 1934) came before Yukawa's meson theory (1935). 'Yukawa and later Fermi' may need to become 'Fermi and later Yukawa'.
post3-p1.idea: This is a long paragraph. Consider splitting it after '…its origins.' and adding a line about how this changed the way you approach your own half-working ideas.
